sections.title: The rule
sections.content: English uses the same shape for *I want to leave* and *I want you to leave*. Spanish uses two different patterns, and the choice depends on who does the second action. You know *querer* and *preferir* from A2 Unit 27, with an infinitive or with *que* + subjunctive (*Quiero comer* / *Quiero que comas*). It works the same way for every kind of verb in this unit: influence, value judgments and feelings.

sections.title: Same subject or different subject?
sections.content: If the person who wants, feels or judges is also the person who acts, use an infinitive. If the second action belongs to someone else, use *que* + subjunctive.

sections.title: One person or two?
rows: I want to leave. / I want you to leave.
Prefiero cenar en casa. / Prefiero que cenemos en casa.
I prefer to have dinner at home. / I prefer that we have dinner at home.
Me alegra estar aquí. / Me alegra que estés aquí.
I'm glad to be here. / I'm glad you are here.
Es importante llegar a tiempo. / Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
It is important to arrive on time. / It is important that you arrive on time.

items.english: My boss hopes to finish today.

items.spanish: Mi jefa espera que terminemos hoy.
items.english: My boss hopes that we finish today.

items.spanish: Ana se negó a firmar el contrato sin leerlo.
items.english: Ana refused to sign the contract without reading it.

items.spanish: Mi hermano pretende que le prestemos el coche.
items.english: My brother expects us to lend him the car.

sections.content: English often hides the second person (*I want him to come*), so ask yourself who does the second action. Same person as the first verb: infinitive. New person: *que* + subjunctive. Verbs like *permitir*, *prohibir* and *aconsejar* are the one place where you may choose, because the other person is named by *me*, *te*, *le*, *nos* or *les*: *Te aconsejo descansar* and *Te aconsejo que descanses* are both correct.
